_note: Ways of delivering household water beside carrying it from a river or spring (water_kg in 50_chemicals.json): drawing from a dug well and piping from a header through lead. Each is a recipe on the materials and trades that do the work, so plumbers, masons and labourers get need from the water households must have (the water need in data/world/needs.json). Water is drawn where it is used, so each states carriage_km zero: the walking and lifting are already in its labour hours. Figures are order-of-magnitude estimates, confidence C or D, none fitted to a headcount.

capital.good: one dug and stone-lined well shaft with windlass, serving about ten households
capital.capital_basis: A shaft about 1.2 m across and 10 m deep is about 11 cubic metres of earth to dig and hoist, at about 15 labourer hours a cubic metre (digging and hoisting from depth, an estimate), so 170 hours. A lining 0.3 m thick on a mean 1.35 m diameter is about 12 cubic metres of laid wall. Lined shafts stand for generations; 50 years is an estimate, no source found. Pass 12 on the digging rate: Stephen Abbott, Hand Dug Wells: Choice of Technology and Construction Manual (sswm.info, https://sswm.info/sites/default/files/reference_attachments/ABBOT%204000%20Hand%20Dug%20Well%20Manual.pdf, opened as text, section 2.2) gives 1.76 cubic metres of excavation a metre of depth for an in-situ lined well and 0.95 for a caisson-lined one, and labour of 'approx. 4 - 8 person days per metre of depth' and 'approx. 2 - 3 person days per metre' respectively, lining included. At ten hours a person-day (the construction data's working day) and 1.76 cubic metres a metre that is 23 to 45 labourer hours a cubic metre including lining and hoisting, against 15 hours for digging alone here (the lining is charged separately as stone_wall_m3 above); within 2x, kept. IRC Special Publication 24 (law.resource.org, https://law.resource.org/pub/in/bis/irc/irc.gov.in.sp.024.1984.pdf, Table 4, opened as text) gives 0.3 to 0.8 man-hours a cubic metre for ordinary soil thrown onto a surface, so the depth hoisting is most of the 15. Ten households of five at 20 litres a head a day draw 50 * 20 * 365 = 365,000 kg a year. Round 4 (Pass 14) tried: comparable (Abbott's manual downloaded and searched for design life, lifespan, years: nothing on how long a lined shaft lasts), rate (digging and lining hours bracketed above), stand-in (Wikipedia, Water well, not opened). Missing: a service life for a stone-lined hand-dug well; 50 years is an assumption, with centuries-old lined wells in use as the only floor.

water_well_kg.basis: per tonne of water drawn from a dug well by bucket and windlass
water_well_kg.yield_basis: A tonne is fifty 20 kg buckets; one drawn from 10 m takes about a minute on a windlass, so about 50 minutes, 0.8 labourer hours. The lift work is only 1000 * 9.81 * 10 = 98 kJ, so time, not energy, is the cost. The well is dearer per tonne than the river bank's carry (water_kg) where the river is close and cheaper where it is far, which this entry does not model; the choice between ways is the household mix's. An estimate of the work rate. Pass 11 partial: Seamus Collins, Hand-dug shallow wells (SKAT, 2000, https://susana.org/_resources/documents/default/3-4183-7-1617201562.pdf, opened as text) describes hand-dug wells 'with a diameter of 1.0-1.5m', excavated at 1.2-1.3 m, which matches the 1.2 m shaft; no source opened for the 20 kg bucket drawn in a minute, the 15 hours a cubic metre of digging or the 50-year life (the IISc and WaterAid pages that give digging rates returned errors), so conf stays D (the bucket rate and the life are unsourced; the digging rate now has the Abbott figures above). Round 4 (Pass 14) bucket rate, derived from human power. Wikipedia, Human power (opened): 'Over an 8-hour work shift, an average, healthy, well-fed and motivated manual laborer may sustain a mechanical power output of around 75 watts.' Lifting 1000 kg through 10 m is 98 kJ (above), so 98,000 / 75 = 1,300 s = 0.36 labourer hours of pure lifting; the held 0.8 hours is 2.2 times that, the allowance for lowering the bucket, filling and emptying it and the windlass losses (labelled assumption), inside 3x of the physical minimum. Digging rate: Abbott and IRC figures in the capital row. The well's life stays unsourced in the capital row.

capital.good: about 200 m of quinaria-class lead pipe laid in a trench with its fittings
capital.capital_basis: Smith's Dictionary (Fistula) and Vitruvius 8.6.4 give the series: 12 Roman pounds per digit of plate width per ten-foot length, so 60 pounds for the five-digit quinaria, about 19.6 kg (a Roman pound is about 0.327 kg) over 2.96 m, about 6.6 kg a metre; 200 m is 1320 kg of lead. A plumber rolled the plate, soldered the seam and joined the lengths: about six hours a ten-foot length, 67 lengths, about 400 hours. Trenching and backfill are about 1.5 labourer hours a metre. The length per stream of flow, the hours and the 50-year life are estimates; lead pipe lasted far longer where the water left no sinter.

capital.good: the water-carrying channel, header cistern and settling tank that feed one quinaria of flow
capital.capital_basis: An aqueduct is about 2000 cubic metres of masonry a kilometre averaged over buried channel and arcade; a 50 km line feeding about four thousand quinariae of flow is about 25 cubic metres of laid wall for each. Both the masonry rate and the flow it feeds are estimates, and a short conduit from a spring needs far less; the labourer hours are for digging and centring. Pass 12 check of the masonry per kilometre: Wikipedia, Roman aqueduct (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_aqueduct, opened): channel 'approximately 0.7 m wide and 1.5 m high internally', 780 to 800 km of conduit for the eleven aqueducts of Rome of which 'approximately 47 km' (6 percent) were above ground on masonry supports. With ASSUMED walls 0.4 m thick and floor and vault 0.2 m each, the solid section is (0.7 + 0.8) * (1.5 + 0.4) - 0.7 * 1.5 = 1.8 square metres, 1800 cubic metres a kilometre of channel. Wikipedia, Pont du Gard (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pont_du_Gard, opened): 'some 21,000 m3' of stone in a bridge 275 m long, 76 cubic metres a metre, the tallest case; at 6 percent arcade that is up to 4600 cubic metres a kilometre added to the average, so 1800 to 6400 against 2000 here, within 3.2x at the top, kept. Flow fed: Wikipedia, Aqua Marcia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqua_Marcia, opened): 91 km long, 4690 quinariae at its source (Frontinus), so 91 * 2000 / 4690 = 39 cubic metres a quinaria against 25 here (within 2x). The cistern and settling tank are not in these figures. Round 4 (Pass 14) tried: comparable (Roman aqueduct, Pont du Gard and Aqua Marcia, above, for masonry per quinaria, 39 against 25 held), rate (IRC Special Publication 24, above, 0.3 to 0.8 hours a cubic metre for throwing earth: a trench of 1.5 m by 2 m (assumed) is 3000 m3 a kilometre, 58 m3 a quinaria at 51 quinariae a kilometre, or 17 to 46 hours of digging against the 300 labourer hours held, so centring and haulage would make up the rest), stand-in (none for centring and the settling tank). Missing: timber centring hours and the size of the header cistern and settling tank.

water_piped_kg.extracted_from: a spring or aqueduct head (the water itself is a natural endowment)
water_piped_kg.basis: per year of one laid quinaria-class lead pipe delivering at full flow
water_piped_kg.yield_basis: A quinaria pipe (five quarter-digits of bore, 2.3 cm) is the unit Frontinus delivers in; one runs about 40 cubic metres a day (Encyclopaedia Romana, Quinaria, penelope.uchicago.edu/~grout/encyclopaedia_romana/romanurbs/quinaria.html, opened: bore "2.3 centimeters", Di Fenizio "almost 0.48 liters per second (approximately 41.5 cubic meters/day)", Taylor "32.8 m3/day"; Frontinus, De aquis 25, Bennett, opened: the quinaria has a diameter of 5/4 of a digit), so 40 * 365 = 14,600 cubic metres, 14,600,000 kg, a year at full flow. Full flow is an upper bound on use, taken as the waterwheel entry takes continuous operation. Upkeep is a gang's work: Frontinus lists a public gang of 240 and Caesar's of 460 slaves for the aqueducts that delivered 14,018 quinariae, about 0.05 workers for each, about 100 hours a year at about 2000 hours a worker; the split between plumber, mason and labourer is an estimate. Delivery has almost no running cost, so per tonne piped water costs a small fraction of a tonne carried by hand wherever the flow is used.
